value.name: Sow
value.user_action_beginner: Scatter arugula seed thickly and evenly across a tray of pre-moistened growing mix, aiming for a dense single layer (about 10 grams, or two teaspoons, per standard 10 by 20 inch tray). Do not soak these small seeds first; just mist the surface with water. Unlike garden planting, microgreens are sown shoulder to shoulder on top of the mix, not spaced out or buried.
value.what_to_look_for_beginner: An even, dense scatter of seed across the whole surface with no bare patches and no thick clumps. The mix underneath should look evenly damp and dark, not soggy or pooling.
value.log_prompt_beginner: Tray sown and misted?
value.user_action_seasoned: Broadcast about 10 g of seed per 1020 tray in a dense, even layer on pre-moistened medium. No presoak for small brassica seed; mist the surface to settle it. Surface-sow, do not cover with mix.
value.what_to_look_for_seasoned: A uniform, dense seed layer with no gaps or clumping on evenly moist medium.

value.name: Germination
value.user_action_beginner: Cover the tray to keep it dark and humid, and set a second empty tray with a light weight (a couple of pounds) on top; the gentle pressure pushes roots down into the mix and gives you a fuller, more even stand. Keep it somewhere warm, around 74°F. Mist if the surface starts to look dry, but do not let it get waterlogged.
value.what_to_look_for_beginner: The seeds swell, split, and push out tiny white roots, then pale looped stems that lift the cover slightly. Under the cover everything looks pale and leggy, which is exactly right at this stage.
value.log_prompt_beginner: Any little sprouts under the cover yet?
value.user_action_seasoned: Stack a weighted blackout cover (a few pounds) over the tray at around 74°F. The weight drives root contact and evens germination. Mist only to keep the surface from drying; avoid saturation.
value.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Seeds imbibe and split; white radicles emerge, followed by pale hooked hypocotyls lifting the weighted cover.

value.name: Blackout
value.user_action_beginner: Keep the tray covered and in the dark for another day or two after most seeds have sprouted. This short dark stretch makes all the stems reach upward together, so they grow tall and even instead of short and patchy. Keep misting lightly if the surface dries.
value.what_to_look_for_beginner: A dense mat of pale, stretched stems standing tall and lifting the cover. The stems will be yellowish or white, not green yet, and that is normal in the dark.
value.log_prompt_beginner: Stems tall and even under there?
value.user_action_seasoned: Hold the blackout cover 1 to 2 days post-germination for arugula. The dark period elongates hypocotyls uniformly and evens the stand before light. Mist to maintain surface moisture.
value.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Uniformly elongated, blanched stems lifting the cover; a tall, even stand pre-greening.

value.name: Light
value.user_action_beginner: Take the cover off and move the tray into bright light, ideally about 18 hours a day, at a comfortable room temperature around 68 to 72°F. The pale stems will green up fast. Switch to watering from the bottom now (pour water into the tray beneath) rather than misting the leaves, which helps prevent mold as the canopy fills in.
value.what_to_look_for_beginner: The stems and seed leaves turn from pale to bright green within a day or so. Soon a small, ruffled first true leaf may appear at the center, and the tray starts to smell peppery.
value.log_prompt_beginner: Are they greening up nicely?
value.user_action_seasoned: Uncover into about 18 hours of light at 68-72°F. Cotyledons green rapidly and the first true leaf may begin. Bottom-water from here to keep the canopy dry and suppress damping-off.
value.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Rapid greening of cotyledons; first true leaf may form. Peppery aroma develops.

value.name: Harvest
value.user_action_beginner: Harvest when the seed leaves are open and green, usually about 6 to 8 days after sowing, with or without a first true leaf. Gather a handful and cut the stems just above the soil line with clean scissors. Rinse gently and eat them fresh; microgreens do not regrow after cutting, so harvest the whole tray.
value.what_to_look_for_beginner: Open, fully green seed leaves standing about one to two inches tall, sometimes with a tiny true leaf just showing. They should taste bright and peppery.
value.log_prompt_beginner: Time to snip and taste? Log your harvest.
value.user_action_seasoned: Single-cut at the cotyledon to first-true-leaf stage, about 6 to 8 days. Cut just above the medium with clean scissors, rinse, and refrigerate or eat fresh. No regrowth; harvest the full tray.
value.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Cotyledons fully expanded and green at 1-2 in, first true leaf just emerging; peppery flavor developed.

value.what_to_look_for_beginner: Big, round seeds spread in a thick, even layer across the whole surface, over evenly damp mix with no pooling water.

value.user_action_seasoned: Dry-broadcast large radish seed densely on pre-moistened medium, roughly 40 g per 1020 tray, in a single even layer. No presoak; mist to settle. Surface-sow.
value.what_to_look_for_seasoned: A dense, even layer of large seed with no gaps on moist medium.

value.name: Germination
value.user_action_beginner: Cover the tray to keep it dark and humid, with a lightly weighted empty tray on top to root the seeds down evenly. Keep it warm, around 70 to 75°F. Radish is one of the easiest microgreens, germinating strongly and evenly, so expect quick action. Mist only if the surface dries.
value.what_to_look_for_beginner: The big seeds swelling, splitting, and pushing out thick white roots, then sturdy pale stems that lift the cover, usually all at once.
value.log_prompt_beginner: Any sprouts pushing up already?
value.user_action_seasoned: Weighted blackout cover at 70-75°F. Large radish seed imbibes and splits fast, with strong, even germination. Mist only to prevent surface drying.
value.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Rapid, uniform imbibition; thick radicles and blanched stems lifting the cover.

value.name: Blackout
value.user_action_beginner: Keep the tray covered in the dark for a short stretch, about one to three days after sprouting. Radish stretches fast, so it needs less dark time than most. This brief dark period evens out the stand before light. Keep misting lightly if the surface dries.
value.what_to_look_for_beginner: A thick mat of pale, stretched stems standing tall and lifting the cover. They will be white or pale pink, not green yet.
value.log_prompt_beginner: Stems tall and even under there?
value.user_action_seasoned: Hold blackout about 1 to 3 days; radish elongates quickly and needs a shorter dark period than slower crops. Mist to maintain surface moisture.
value.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Uniformly elongated, blanched (often pink-tinged) stems lifting the cover.

value.name: Light
value.user_action_beginner: Uncover the tray and move it into bright light, about 18 hours a day, at a comfortable 68 to 72°F. The pale stems green up fast, and many varieties keep a pretty pink or purple tint on the stems. Water from the bottom now instead of misting the leaves to keep the canopy dry.
value.what_to_look_for_beginner: Seed leaves turning bright green within a day, often over pink or purple stems, and the tray taking on a sharp, spicy smell.
value.log_prompt_beginner: Greening up, with pink stems showing?
value.user_action_seasoned: Uncover into about 18 hours of light at 68-72°F. Cotyledons green rapidly; stems often retain pink or purple pigment. Bottom-water to keep the canopy dry.
value.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Rapid greening of cotyledons over pigmented stems; pungent aroma develops.

value.name: Harvest
value.user_action_beginner: Harvest when the seed leaves are open and green, usually about a week after sowing. Gather a handful and cut just above the soil line with clean scissors. Radish microgreens pack a spicy, peppery kick; eat them fresh, and remember they do not regrow, so cut the whole tray.
value.what_to_look_for_beginner: Open green seed leaves about one to two inches tall, on colorful stems, with a bold peppery bite when you taste one.
value.log_prompt_beginner: Time to snip that spice? Log your harvest.
value.user_action_seasoned: Single-cut at the cotyledon to first-true-leaf stage, often about 7 days. Cut just above the medium with clean scissors, rinse, and use fresh. Pungent flavor. No regrowth; harvest the full tray.
value.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Cotyledons open at 1-2 in on pigmented stems; sharp, peppery flavor.

from.description_seasoned: Presoak seed 8 to 12 hours, then broadcast densely and evenly on pre-moistened medium; do not bury.
from.description_beginner: Soak the seed 8 to 12 hours, then scatter it thickly on damp medium; do not cover with soil.

from.description_seasoned: Seeds imbibe and root under a covered, weighted tray at about 74 °F.
from.description_beginner: Seeds sprout under a covered, weighted, warm tray.

from.description_seasoned: About 3 to 4 dark days under 2 to 5 pounds of weight that stretch the stems evenly and help the hulls split off the cotyledons.
from.description_beginner: About 3 to 4 days in the dark under a weight, which makes the stems stretch evenly and helps the shells come off.

from.description_seasoned: Uncovered into about 18 hours of light at about 72 °F; cotyledons green and plump, and any clinging hulls are rubbed or rinsed off.
from.description_beginner: Uncovered into bright light so the seed leaves turn green; brush off any leftover shells.

from.description_seasoned: Single cut at the base at the plump-cotyledon stage, before the first true leaves expand; eaten fresh.
from.description_beginner: Snip at the base when the seed leaves are full and before true leaves form; eat fresh.

value.name: Sow
value.user_action_beginner: Sunflower seeds are large, so soak them first: cover them with cool water for 8 to 12 hours, then drain. Scatter the drained seed thickly and evenly across a tray of pre-moistened mix in a dense single layer. Do not bury them; they sit right on top of the mix. A crowded, even layer helps the seedlings push their seed coats off later.
value.what_to_look_for_beginner: Plump, swollen seeds spread in a thick, even layer across the surface, over damp mix with no standing water.
value.log_prompt_beginner: Seeds soaked and sown?
value.user_action_seasoned: Presoak seed 8 to 12 hours, drain, then broadcast densely and evenly on pre-moistened medium in a single layer. Do not cover with mix. A dense stand aids hull shedding downstream.
value.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Fully imbibed, swollen seed in a dense even layer on moist, well-drained medium.

value.name: Germination
value.user_action_beginner: Cover the tray to keep it dark, and set a weighted empty tray on top; sunflowers need real weight to root down and to help split their seed coats. Keep it warm, around 74°F. Mist if the surface dries, but do not let it get soggy.
value.what_to_look_for_beginner: Seeds splitting and pushing out thick white roots, then sturdy pale stems, many still wearing their black-and-white seed coats like little helmets.
value.log_prompt_beginner: Any sprouts pushing up the cover?
value.user_action_seasoned: Weighted blackout cover at around 74°F; sunflowers benefit from firm weight for rooting and hull splitting. Mist only to prevent surface drying.
value.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Radicles emerge and thick blanched stems lift the cover; many hypocotyls still bearing pericarps (hulls).

value.name: Blackout
value.user_action_beginner: Keep the tray covered and weighted in the dark for about three to four days after sprouting. Use 2 to 5 pounds of weight (a second tray with a brick or a water jug works). The weight makes the stems push up strong and even, and it helps pop the seed coats off the leaves. Mist lightly if the surface dries.
value.what_to_look_for_beginner: Tall, pale, sturdy stems lifting the weighted cover together, many shedding or ready to shed their seed coats. Still pale, not green.
value.log_prompt_beginner: Stems tall and shedding their shells?
value.user_action_seasoned: Hold weighted blackout about 3 to 4 days under 2 to 5 lb. The weight elongates stems evenly and helps shear the hulls off the cotyledons. Mist to maintain surface moisture.
value.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Uniformly elongated blanched stems lifting the weight; hulls loosening or dropping from cotyledons.

value.name: Light
value.user_action_beginner: Uncover the tray and move it into bright light, about 18 hours a day, around 72°F. The seed leaves plump up and turn green. Gently rub or rinse off any seed coats still clinging to the leaves; leaving them on invites mold. Water from the bottom now rather than over the leaves.
value.what_to_look_for_beginner: Thick, plump seed leaves turning deep green, standing on crisp white stems, with the last black seed coats brushing off easily.
value.log_prompt_beginner: Greening up, shells brushed off?
value.user_action_seasoned: Uncover into about 18 hours of light at around 72°F. Cotyledons green and plump. Rub or rinse off clinging hulls to prevent mold. Bottom-water to keep the canopy dry.
value.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Cotyledons greening and thickening; residual hulls shed; crisp white hypocotyls.

value.name: Harvest
value.user_action_beginner: Harvest at the plump seed-leaf stage, before the first true leaves open, usually about 8 to 14 days. Wait too long and the shoots turn bitter. Cut just above the soil line with clean scissors. Sunflower shoots are thick, crunchy, and nutty; eat them fresh, and cut the whole tray since they do not regrow.
value.what_to_look_for_beginner: Fat, green seed leaves on thick crunchy stems two to four inches tall, with no true leaves showing yet. They should taste nutty and fresh, not bitter.
value.log_prompt_beginner: Plump and ready before they turn? Log your harvest.
value.user_action_seasoned: Single-cut at the base at the plump-cotyledon stage, before true leaves expand, about 8 to 14 days; later cuts turn bitter. Cut with clean scissors, rinse, and use fresh. No regrowth; harvest the full tray.
value.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Plump green cotyledons on thick stems, pre-true-leaf; nutty, crunchy, not yet bitter.
value.log_prompt_seasoned: Cutting before true leaves? Log your harvest.

from.description_seasoned: Wheat berries soaked 8 to 12 hours (optionally sprouted a day), then spread thickly in an even single layer on pre-moistened medium.
from.description_beginner: Wheat berries soaked for 8 to 12 hours, then spread in one even layer on damp medium.

from.description_seasoned: Seeds root and sprout under a covered tray at about 60 to 70 °F.
from.description_beginner: Seeds sprout under a covered tray in a warm room.

from.description_seasoned: Short dark period (about 2 to 3 days) that evens the stand and stretches the young shoots before light.
from.description_beginner: A couple of days in the dark that bring the grass up evenly before you give it light.

from.description_seasoned: Uncovered into bright indirect light; the blades green up and grow toward cutting height.
from.description_beginner: Uncovered into bright light so the grass turns deep green and grows tall.

from.description_seasoned: Single cut near the base at about 6 to 7 inches, at the jointing stage when a second blade begins; juiced fresh.
from.description_beginner: Cut the grass near the soil at about 6 to 7 inches tall, then juice it fresh.

value.name: Sow
value.user_action_beginner: Soak wheat berries in cool water for 8 to 12 hours, then drain. Spread the drained berries in a single even layer across a tray of pre-moistened mix, close together but ideally not piled in a thick heap, which can trap moisture and cause mold. Wheatgrass is grown for juicing, so a clean, even mat is the goal.
value.what_to_look_for_beginner: Plump, swollen wheat berries spread in one even layer across the surface, over damp mix with no standing water and no thick clumps.
value.log_prompt_beginner: Berries soaked and spread?
value.user_action_seasoned: Soak wheat berries 8 to 12 hours (optionally pre-sprout one day), drain, then spread in a dense single layer on pre-moistened medium. Avoid deep piling, which promotes matting and mold. Surface-sow.
value.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Fully imbibed berries in a single even layer on moist, well-drained medium; no deep piles.

value.name: Germination
value.user_action_beginner: Cover the tray to keep it dark and humid while the berries root and sprout. Keep it in a warm room, around 60 to 70°F. Wheatgrass roots into a dense mat, so give it a little airflow and mist only lightly; a constantly wet mat is the main cause of mold at the base.
value.what_to_look_for_beginner: White roots knitting into a mat across the tray, then pale green-tipped shoots beginning to stand up under the cover.
value.log_prompt_beginner: Roots and shoots starting under the cover?
value.user_action_seasoned: Cover for darkness at 60-70°F while berries root and sprout. The dense root mat is mold-prone; favor light misting and airflow over saturation.
value.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Roots forming a mat; blanched shoots with green tips emerging under the cover.

value.name: Blackout
value.user_action_beginner: Keep the tray covered in the dark for a couple of days after sprouting to bring the grass up tall and even before it sees light. Watch the base of the mat closely: if it stays soggy it can grow moldy, so keep airflow going and do not overwater.
value.what_to_look_for_beginner: A dense stand of pale, upright shoots several inches tall lifting the cover, growing evenly together. Still pale, not deep green.
value.log_prompt_beginner: Grass coming up tall and even?
value.user_action_seasoned: Hold blackout about 2 to 3 days to even the stand and elongate shoots. Monitor the root mat for saturation; airflow is the primary mold control.
value.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Uniform, elongated pale shoots lifting the cover; dense even stand pre-greening.

value.name: Light
value.user_action_beginner: Uncover the tray and move it into bright, indirect light. The blades turn deep green and grow toward cutting height. Keep watering from the bottom or lightly at the base, never soaking the crowns, and keep the air moving to hold mold off the dense mat.
value.what_to_look_for_beginner: Blades turning from pale to deep, rich green and standing tall, growing noticeably taller each day.
value.log_prompt_beginner: Turning deep green and growing tall?
value.user_action_seasoned: Uncover into bright indirect light. Blades green and gain height. Bottom-water and maintain airflow; avoid crown wetting on the dense mat.
value.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Blades greening to deep green and elongating toward cutting height.

value.name: Harvest
value.user_action_beginner: Cut when the grass is about 6 to 7 inches tall and just starting to split into a second blade (the jointing stage), usually 7 to 10 days in. Snip near the base with clean scissors and juice it fresh right away; wheatgrass is juiced, not eaten whole. One good cut is standard, and a tray may offer a lighter second cut before it fades.
value.what_to_look_for_beginner: Deep green blades six to seven inches tall, with a second blade just beginning to appear from the center. That jointing point is peak sweetness for juicing.
value.log_prompt_beginner: Tall enough to cut and juice? Log it.
value.user_action_seasoned: Single-cut near the base at about 6 to 7 inches, at the jointing stage as the second blade begins, roughly 7 to 10 days. Juice fresh immediately. A modest second cut is sometimes possible before decline.
value.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Blades at 6-7 in with a second blade initiating (jointing); optimal juicing point.
value.log_prompt_seasoned: Cutting at jointing? Log your harvest.
